Commentary: Affordability Is the Top Issue on California’s November Ballot
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/) and Ian Klaus (https://www.ppic.org/person/ian-klaus/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Mark Baldassare , (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Ian Klaus (https://www.ppic.org/person/ian-klaus/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/) and Ian Klaus (https://www.ppic.org/person/ian-klaus/)
An earlier version of this commentary (https://carnegieendowment.org/posts/2026/07/california-november-ballot-affordability-fiscal-priorities) was published by Carnegie California (https://carnegieendowment.org/programs/carnegie-california) on July 28, 2026.
California is widely expected to live up to its blue-state reputation in the November election for governor and other statewide races. The latest PPIC Statewide Survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) shows that Democrats hold a twenty-point advantage in partisan voter registration (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2026-news-releases-and-advisories/california-secretary-state-shirley-n-weber-phd-releases-may-18-2026-report-registration), and no Republican has won a statewide race since 2006 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2006-general/sum_amended.pdf).
But plenty of important, open issues still will be decided by voters this fall. Further down on the ballot—where choosing between a Democratic or Republican candidate is replaced by a “Yes” or “No” vote—fourteen state propositions (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2026-news-releases-and-advisories/secretary-state-shirley-n-weber-phd-assigns-numbers-november-ballot-measures-invites-ballot-arguments)’ outcomes will provide insight into how voters think about affordability, federal uncertainty, and election reforms in advance of the next presidential election.
This year’s mix of nine citizens’ initiatives supported by a variety of interest groups and five legislative measures is the most on the state ballot since 2016 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/06-sov-summary.pdf) and represents the latest and arguably the biggest test for California’s direct democracy system. We know (https://www.ppic.org/blog/reengaging-citizens-in-the-initiative-process/) California voters like being able to make policy decisions at the ballot box, but the number and complexity of state propositions can be overwhelming. And despite the state’s reputation for governmental intervention, the historical default is for Californians to vote no if they have doubts about the policy outcomes.
With that context in mind, we’ve grouped thematically the key propositions that will provide insight into California—and national politics—looking forward.
Affordability in the Golden State: Propositions 1, 3, 37, 40, 41, 42, 45
When asked in a recent PPIC Statewide Survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) to name the most important issue facing the people of California today, Californians chose affordability and the cost of living, followed by housing costs and availability. Many voters expressed concerns about their own financial situations (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-december-2025/) and housing costs in their regions (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-december-2025/). Our recent Carnegie California survey (https://carnegieendowment.org/emissary/2025/12/openai-california-ai-ballot-direct-democracy) shows that a majority of Californians worry that AI—including the IPOs of OpenAI and Anthropic later this year—will worsen inequality. Majorities also prefer to have lower taxes and raise state taxes on wealthy Californians to pay for state programs today. This explains the context for half of the California ballot items this fall.
The affordability measure with the highest profile on the November ballot is Proposition 40 . This is a labor union–sponsored initiative that would impose a one-time tax of up to 5 percent on individuals’ assets of over $1 billion to pay for healthcare, food assistance, and education-related programs. This initiative spawned two business-sponsored initiatives ( Propositions 41 and 42 ) that are specifically designed to counter the legality and implementation of the billionaire tax if it passes. Proposition 3 is another labor union–sponsored initiative that would make permanent a temporary tax on high incomes to fund schools and healthcare that voters passed in 2012 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/06-sov-summary.pdf) with an end date of 2018 and that voters passed again in 2016 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/06-sov-summary.pdf) with an end date of 2030. Early polling finds that majorities of likely voters would vote yes (54 percent (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)) on the billionaire tax and yes (62 percent (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-education-april-2026/)) on permanently extending the tax on high incomes.
Turning to housing affordability, Proposition 1 is the $11.250 billion state bond measure placed on the ballot by the legislature to finance programs to fund affordable rental housing and homeownership programs. Proposition 37 is a citizens’ initiative sponsored by real estate interests and labor unions that would authorize up to $25 billion in bonds for middle-income buyers of qualified new homes to be paid by homeowners’ mortgage payments.
These massive state bonds share the November ballot with the business-sponsored Proposition 45 that would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review of certain projects, including most housing. Early polling finds that about half or more of the likely voters would vote yes on a multibillion-dollar state housing bond (49 percent (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/)) and the middle-class loan program (53 percent (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), while overwhelming majorities would vote yes (73 percent (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/)) on the CEQA reform to speed up housing reviews. This adds up to the most ambitious collection of housing propositions in recent memory.
Federal Uncertainty and Fiscal Priorities: Propositions 2, 38, 44
A host of executive orders and the One Big Beautiful Bill that Congress passed in 2025 have resulted in uncertainty about federal funding for state government programs. California’s health programs and research grants are especially vulnerable to federal cuts. This puts the state and its voters in a very tough place. Majorities of likely voters in recent PPIC polling (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0526.pdf) say they want the California government to backfill the loss of federal funding, but they are not willing to pay higher taxes. How will Californians balance these often-competing viewpoints? Several proposals for dealing with federal uncertainty will appear on the November ballot.
Proposition 2 is a legislative measure that would increase the share of state tax revenues collected each year that could be set aside for future use from 10 percent to 20 percent. This rainy-day-fund increase aims to prepare for budget gaps from federal cuts and revenue decreases. PPIC’s recent polling finds that likely voters (70 percent (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0526.pdf)) are in favor of raising the cap. Proposition 38 is a citizens’ initiative sponsored by philanthropists and medical associations that would authorize a $8.4 billion state bond for immunology and immunotherapy research. Proposition 44 is a labor union–sponsored initiative that would require community health clinics to spend 90 percent of revenues on services. Together, these propositions would backfill federal funding gaps in ways that appear consistent with the priorities of Californians more generally, but they would be costly.
Election Reforms and California’s Democracy: Propositions 4, 5, 39, 43
When asked in a recent PPIC Statewide Survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) to name the most important problem facing the nation today, Californians chose threats to democracy and political extremism. Most California voters are not satisfied with the way democracy in the United States (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-december-2025/) is working, and many express concerns about voting and elections in the state (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Californians’ views about elections have also been influenced by recent voting experiences, such as the 2021 governor’s recall, when voters were asked to keep or remove their governor and choose a replacement on the same ballot. In this context, proposals for changes to state and local elections are on the ballot in November.
Proposition 4 is a legislative measure that would allow state and local governments to create programs for state and local candidates to receive public funds within certain limits. It would amend the 1974 state law (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/about-fppc/about-the-political-reform-act/) passed by voters that prohibits the use of public funds for campaigning. Proposition 5 is also a legislative measure that would change the governor’s recall election to a single vote for removing or keeping the current officeholder. Proposition 39 is a citizens’ initiative that was sponsored by two GOP legislators that would establish additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. Proposition 43 is a legislative measure that would require a two-thirds majority rather than a simple majority vote to pass a special local tax.
We don’t have any recent polling on public financing of state and local campaigns or changes in the governor’s recall election. About half of likely voters (49 percent (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)) say they would vote yes on the voter identification requirements, while fewer (39 percent (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-education-april-2026/)) would vote yes on the local tax limitations, with partisans deeply divided on these two measures. It’s noteworthy that Proposition 43 was part of a legislative compromise resulting in proponents withdrawing their citizens’ initiative for local tax limits.
What’s Not on the Ballot
California voters were spared from a twenty-one-measure state ballot when seven citizens’ initiatives (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/failed-qualify) were withdrawn by proponents or failed to gather the required number of signatures. In a year when affordability has an outsized role on the ballot, advocates of minimum-wage increases and local rent controls took a pass in the wake of their citizens’ initiatives being rejected in November 2024 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/65-official-dec-vote-results-bm.pdf).
It’s also noteworthy that the issue of artificial intelligence regulation is not on the ballot, as child AI safety advocates and OpenAI agreed to work together (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/09/openai-heads-for-deal-with-kids-safety-group-on-california-ballot-measure-00719158) rather than submitting dueling initiatives. Meanwhile, citizen input on AI is being gathered by Engaged California (https://engaged.ca.gov/ai-impact/) that could inform future legislative measures. A recent Carnegie California Survey shows that Californians considered AI policy important when voting in the gubernatorial primary, but the essential questions around the impacts of the emerging technology have yet to work their way through the established direct democracy system.
What’s Next?
California voters face a daunting November ballot, with choices on fourteen state propositions. They will be subject to a tidal wave of television commercials, social media posts, and mail from those campaigns. In their search for trusted information, the State Voter Information Guide (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/publications-and-resources/state-county-vig) will be the go-to source.
California and about half of other states (https://ballotpedia.org/States_with_initiative_or_referendum) have initiatives and referendums, and most state legislatures can ask voters to make and change policies. Voters’ experiences with their state’s direct democracy will have a role in their views about how well US democracy is working in this consequential midterm. We will report back on the California ballot outcomes after the November election.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm noting the PPIC numbers: 49% yes in February, which was early polling before the measure was specified, then 55% yes in September, and 60% yes in mid-October. This is a bond measure with no organized opposition, since the voter guide has no opposition argument and the No campaign has reported no contributions, and I'm weighing what that means for the outlook.

I'm checking how the opposition in the Legislature breaks down, a few Republican votes against, which makes the opposition look minor. Looking back at past California bond measures, they usually pass, though some, like the 2020 school bond and a 2018 water bond, have failed.

I'm going through the historical record of California bond measures from 2002 to 2000, noting that most passed with majorities in the high 50s to mid 60s, while a few failed in the 1990s.

I'm checking the 1990s bond record as well, where a few measures failed, such as a 1994 earthquake school bond and a transit bond. I'm estimating that roughly 85 to 90 percent of legislatively referred bonds pass, though the mood can turn sour. With the October poll at 60 percent yes among likely voters, the measure looks likely to pass, and I'm weighing whether bond polls tend to overstate support by a few points.

I'm comparing the polls against actual results for recent California bond measures, and they often differ. For the March 2024 Prop 1, a February poll had 56% yes but the measure got 50.2%, so polls can overstate support by several points.

I'm checking the 2020 Prop 13 case, where the poll had it near the final result but the measure still lost, and I'm estimating that even a six-point drop from the 60% October figure would leave it around 54%, still passing. I'm also wondering whether the election has already happened and whether post-election coverage might show the actual outcome.

I'm checking whether the election has already happened, looking for the Secretary of State's results page to see if the outcome is posted.
PPIC's numbers check out: 55% Yes in September and 60% Yes in October. I'll look for actual election results from the Secretary of State and news outlets, in case voting has already happened.

I'm going through the historical record of California bond measures from 2002 to 2000, noting that most passed with majorities in the high 50s to mid 60s, while a few failed in the 1990s.

I'm checking the 1990s bond record as well, where a few measures failed, such as a 1994 earthquake school bond and a transit bond. I'm estimating that roughly 85 to 90 percent of legislatively referred bonds pass, though the mood can turn sour. With the October poll at 60 percent yes among likely voters, the measure looks likely to pass, and I'm weighing whether bond polls tend to overstate support by a few points.

I'm comparing the polls against actual results for recent California bond measures, and they often differ. For the March 2024 Prop 1, a February poll had 56% yes but the measure got 50.2%, so polls can overstate support by several points.

I'm checking the 2020 Prop 13 case, where the poll had it near the final result but the measure still lost, and I'm estimating that even a six-point drop from the 60% October figure would leave it around 54%, still passing. I'm also wondering whether the election has already happened and whether post-election coverage might show the actual outcome.

I'm checking whether the election has already happened, looking for the Secretary of State's results page to see if the outcome is posted.

I'm noting the PPIC numbers: 49% yes in February, which was early polling before the measure was specified, then 55% yes in September, and 60% yes in mid-October. This is a bond measure with no organized opposition, since the voter guide has no opposition argument and the No campaign has reported no contributions, and I'm weighing what that means for the outlook.

I'm checking how the opposition in the Legislature breaks down, a few Republican votes against, which makes the opposition look minor. Looking back at past California bond measures, they usually pass, though some, like the 2020 school bond and a 2018 water bond, have failed.

I'm going through the historical record of California bond measures from 2002 to 2000, noting that most passed with majorities in the high 50s to mid 60s, while a few failed in the 1990s.

I'm checking the 1990s bond record as well, where a few measures failed, such as a 1994 earthquake school bond and a transit bond. I'm estimating that roughly 85 to 90 percent of legislatively referred bonds pass, though the mood can turn sour. With the October poll at 60 percent yes among likely voters, the measure looks likely to pass, and I'm weighing whether bond polls tend to overstate support by a few points.

I'm comparing the polls against actual results for recent California bond measures, and they often differ. For the March 2024 Prop 1, a February poll had 56% yes but the measure got 50.2%, so polls can overstate support by several points.

I'm checking the 2020 Prop 13 case, where the poll had it near the final result but the measure still lost, and I'm estimating that even a six-point drop from the 60% October figure would leave it around 54%, still passing. I'm also wondering whether the election has already happened and whether post-election coverage might show the actual outcome.

I'm checking whether the election has already happened, looking for the Secretary of State's results page to see if the outcome is posted.

content.text: PPIC's numbers check out: 55% Yes in September and 60% Yes in October. I'll look for actual election results from the Secretary of State and news outlets, in case voting has already happened.

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Proposition 1
Borrow $11.25 billion for housing
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Proposition 1
Borrow $11.25 billion for housing
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

New poll shows billionaire tax falling behind as election nears
by
Lynn La (https://calmatters.org/author/lynn-la/)
October 28, 2026 October 27, 2026
A “Tax the Ultra-Rich Now” bus parked in San Francisco on Oct. 3, 2026. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters
Californians’ appetite for a first-in-the-nation wealth tax appears to be waning.
With less than a week before Election Day, support for Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), a proposed billionaire tax, is now under water, according to the latest poll by Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). Published Tuesday, the survey found that 46% of 1,086 likely voters support the tax, while 52% don’t.
That’s a notable change from last month, when Prop. 40 proponents held a slim 52% majority. The billionaire tax is by far the biggest and most expensive fight on the ballot. As of mid-October, wealthy people who oppose it have raised more than $205 million to fight the tax, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who has poured at least $102 million.
Still, Prop. 40 supporters remain undeterred. In response to the PPIC poll, Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union behind the measure, said “large majorities of Democratic voters” continue to support it.
Jimenez , in an email to CalMatters: “Even after months of the most controversial billionaires on the planet spending millions to spread misinformation about it, a clear majority of voters support asking about 250 billionaires to pay a modest, one-time tax to keep … healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.”
Meanwhile, a pair of related ballot measures intended to negate the billionaire tax could go either way.
Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), with 51% in support among those polled, holds onto a narrow lead. It would bar new taxes on personal property and assets and prohibit retroactive taxes. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), which would impose limits to certain new state taxes, appears to be falling short with 48% support.
Voters seem to be more favorable on five other ballot measures (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/last-minute-voter-guide-propositions/). A majority of survey participants said they would vote yes on:
Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/), the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop. 2 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-proposition-2-explained/), which would increase the amount of tax revenue the state can put in savings
Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/), which would permanently extend an income tax for high-earning households
Prop. 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), which would create a $25 billion fund to help homebuyers
Prop. 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), which would dedicate $8 billion in bonds to fund immunology research
As for the governor’s race (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-governor-race-final-stretch/), Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra continues his lead in the polls with PPIC reporting that 61% of likely voters would vote for him, compared to 37% for Republican Steve Hilton.

Where Trump’s CA election lawsuit stands
A polling station clerk sanitizes a voting station at the Monsignor Ramon Garcia Recreation Center in East Los Angeles on Nov. 8, 2022. Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters
A federal judge appeared skeptical about the Trump administration’s demands that California set aside 20,000 ballots from alleged noncitizens, but won’t likely rule on the matter until after the Nov. 3 election (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/trump-noncitizen-voting-court/), report CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow and Nigel Duara.
In a potential setback for President Donald Trump, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter on Tuesday raised concerns that the administration’s efforts to stop noncitizens from illegally voting by ordering the state’s elections officials to sequester their ballots could disenfranchise “valid voters.”
Though he’s expected to issue a formal ruling today, Carter’s final ruling might not come until after another hearing that will take place in two weeks. Carter also suggested that his ruling would prohibit federal authorities from threatening elections officials with criminal charges if they didn’t comply with Trump’s demands.
Read more (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/trump-noncitizen-voting-court/).
Could election results help LA fire survivors?
Construction workers build a house in Altadena on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters
Survivors of the Eaton and Palisades fires are running out of money to rebuild their lives, and the outcome of the midterm elections may affect whether federal aid will come (https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/10/la-fire-survivors-federal-disaster-aid/), writes CalMatters’ Levi Sumagaysay.
Nearly two years since the fires ripped through the Los Angeles area, the Trump administration has been slow to release funding to California, and it didn’t include L.A. County wildfire relief in its budget request for Congress this summer.
It’s also unclear when the billions of dollars in long-term disaster recovery money the state has requested will come — if at all. Last week, outlets reported that the Federal Emergency Management Agency told states they will need to handle most disasters themselves (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/20/fema-states-disasters-exclusive-energy-environment-01128120).
U.S. Reps. Judy Chu and Norma Torres, both Southern California Democrats, said that if Democrats flip the House in November, federal aid could roll out to California and other states hit by disaster.
Read more (https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/10/la-fire-survivors-federal-disaster-aid/).
And lastly: Fresno dad suddenly deported
Luis Arreguin stands at the Cathedral of Mexicali, in Mexicali, Baja California, Mexico, on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Daniel Resendiz for CalMatters
Luis Arreguin, a 54-year-old Fresno resident, was on his way to work as a skilled laborer on Oct. 1 when federal immigration enforcement agents arrested him. Sixteen days later, agents deported him to Mexico — where he hasn’t been since he was a kid — in a stunning example of the dizzying speed in which Trump’s deportation machine operates. Said Arreguin: “My whole life got destroyed.” Read more (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/deportation-after-fresno-sweep/) from CalMatters’ Wendy Fry.

Meet the Berkeley IGS Poll Director
Read Mark DiCamillo's bio here. (https://igs.berkeley.edu/people/mark-dicamillo)
The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).
IGS Poll (2016 - current) and California Field Poll data (1950's to 2015) can be downloaded from UC Berkeley Dataverse (https://datasets.lib.berkeley.edu/dataverse/igs).

2026 California Prop 1 guide: Affordable rentals get $7.2 billion of the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop 1’s supporters stress “no new taxes,” which is true. The General Fund would still repay $10 billion at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Here is what that money buys, and why the $1.25 billion veterans’ share costs the state nothing directly.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 17, 2026

California's Proposition 1 is asking voters to borrow $11.25 billion for affordable rental housing, homebuyers and veterans' home loans.
Proposition 1 would let California borrow $11.25 billion by selling general obligation bonds. Ten billion dollars would go to 11 existing state housing programs and be repaid from the General Fund, mostly to build and preserve apartments rented to low-income households, with the rest for homebuyer help, infrastructure, and farmworker, student and tribal housing. The other $1.25 billion would fund CalVet home loans, which veterans repay through their mortgage payments. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years, roughly a quarter of 1% of the General Fund, and estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental units and help up to 40,000 households with homeownership. The measure creates no new tax; the debt is paid from the state's existing revenue.
The Affordable Housing Bond under Proposition 1 is sending $7.2 billion of its $11.25 billion to rental housing, led by $5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. Prop 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/) placed on the ballot by SB 417, which the Legislature passed and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on June 25. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the third California measure numbered Proposition 1 to borrow for housing since 2018, following the $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond of 2018 and the $6.38 billion behavioral health bond voters approved by 26,223 votes in March 2024. PPIC's September survey found 55% yes and 43% no. No argument against it was filed and no opposition committee exists; the Yes side reports $7.9 million from top donors, including Airbnb, two carpenters' councils, Building a Better California and nonprofit housing developers. This explainer covers where each dollar goes, the veterans' loan bond, the Legislature's power to move money between programs, the cost, the earlier Prop 1s, the money, the argument and the polling.

This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf) has two parts. The first adds Part 16.1 to the Health and Safety Code, creating the Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 and authorizing $10 billion in bonds that are "a valid and binding general obligation of the state," with "the full faith and credit of the state … pledged" to repay them. The second adds an article to the Military and Veterans Code authorizing $1.25 billion in veterans' bonds for the farm and home loan program the Department of Veterans Affairs runs under the Veterans' Farm and Home Purchase Act of 1974. Both sets of bonds are sold over time by state finance committees as programs ask for cash, so the state does not borrow the full amount at once.
Section 54054 divides the $10 billion into 11 lines, each assigned to a program already in state law. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/title-summary.htm) groups them as $5.1 billion for multifamily rental housing, $2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate or preserve affordable housing and provide supportive housing, $1.1 billion for homeownership, $1 billion for farmworker, tribal and student housing, $500 million for infrastructure and $200 million for local programs. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) combines the first two into a single $7.2 billion for affordable multifamily housing. The summary also notes that the money can finance "housing development projects seeking federal tax credits," and the LAO expects most of it to be "used together with other government monies."
Prop 1's $7.2 billion for rental housing runs mostly through the Multifamily Housing Program:
The largest line, $5.1 billion, goes to the Department of Housing and Community Development's Multifamily Housing Program, which lends to developers of new and renovated apartments in exchange for rent limits. The LAO describes these as "low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost," with units generally reserved for low-income households "for a period of 55 years." Prop 1 adds one condition of its own: at least 10% of the assisted units in each development must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
A further $1.15 billion is set aside for supportive housing, where residents get on-site services such as mental health and substance use counseling. The administering agency must offer capitalized operating subsidy reserves for those units, money set aside up front to cover the gap between what very low-income tenants can pay and what the building costs to run. New poll shows billionaire tax falling behind as election nears
by
Lynn La (https://calmatters.org/author/lynn-la/)
October 28, 2026 October 27, 2026
A “Tax the Ultra-Rich Now” bus parked in San Francisco on Oct. 3, 2026. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters
Californians’ appetite for a first-in-the-nation wealth tax appears to be waning.
With less than a week before Election Day, support for Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), a proposed billionaire tax, is now under water, according to the latest poll by Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). Published Tuesday, the survey found that 46% of 1,086 likely voters support the tax, while 52% don’t.
That’s a notable change from last month, when Prop. 40 proponents held a slim 52% majority. The billionaire tax is by far the biggest and most expensive fight on the ballot. As of mid-October, wealthy people who oppose it have raised more than $205 million to fight the tax, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who has poured at least $102 million.
Still, Prop. 40 supporters remain undeterred. In response to the PPIC poll, Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union behind the measure, said “large majorities of Democratic voters” continue to support it.
Jimenez , in an email to CalMatters: “Even after months of the most controversial billionaires on the planet spending millions to spread misinformation about it, a clear majority of voters support asking about 250 billionaires to pay a modest, one-time tax to keep … healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.”
Meanwhile, a pair of related ballot measures intended to negate the billionaire tax could go either way.
Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), with 51% in support among those polled, holds onto a narrow lead. It would bar new taxes on personal property and assets and prohibit retroactive taxes. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), which would impose limits to certain new state taxes, appears to be falling short with 48% support.
Voters seem to be more favorable on five other ballot measures (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/last-minute-voter-guide-propositions/). A majority of survey participants said they would vote yes on:
Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/), the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop. 2 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-proposition-2-explained/), which would increase the amount of tax revenue the state can put in savings
Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/), which would permanently extend an income tax for high-earning households
Prop. 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), which would create a $25 billion fund to help homebuyers
Prop. 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), which would dedicate $8 billion in bonds to fund immunology research
As for the governor’s race (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-governor-race-final-stretch/), Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra continues his lead in the polls with PPIC reporting that 61% of likely voters would vote for him, compared to 37% for Republican Steve Hilton.

Where Trump’s CA election lawsuit stands
A polling station clerk sanitizes a voting station at the Monsignor Ramon Garcia Recreation Center in East Los Angeles on Nov. 8, 2022. Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters
A federal judge appeared skeptical about the Trump administration’s demands that California set aside 20,000 ballots from alleged noncitizens, but won’t likely rule on the matter until after the Nov. 3 election (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/trump-noncitizen-voting-court/), report CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow and Nigel Duara.
In a potential setback for President Donald Trump, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter on Tuesday raised concerns that the administration’s efforts to stop noncitizens from illegally voting by ordering the state’s elections officials to sequester their ballots could disenfranchise “valid voters.”
Though he’s expected to issue a formal ruling today, Carter’s final ruling might not come until after another hearing that will take place in two weeks. Carter also suggested that his ruling would prohibit federal authorities from threatening elections officials with criminal charges if they didn’t comply with Trump’s demands.
Read more (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/trump-noncitizen-voting-court/).
Could election results help LA fire survivors?
Construction workers build a house in Altadena on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters
Survivors of the Eaton and Palisades fires are running out of money to rebuild their lives, and the outcome of the midterm elections may affect whether federal aid will come (https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/10/la-fire-survivors-federal-disaster-aid/), writes CalMatters’ Levi Sumagaysay.
Nearly two years since the fires ripped through the Los Angeles area, the Trump administration has been slow to release funding to California, and it didn’t include L.A. County wildfire relief in its budget request for Congress this summer.
It’s also unclear when the billions of dollars in long-term disaster recovery money the state has requested will come — if at all. Last week, outlets reported that the Federal Emergency Management Agency told states they will need to handle most disasters themselves (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/20/fema-states-disasters-exclusive-energy-environment-01128120).
U.S. Reps. Judy Chu and Norma Torres, both Southern California Democrats, said that if Democrats flip the House in November, federal aid could roll out to California and other states hit by disaster.
Read more (https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/10/la-fire-survivors-federal-disaster-aid/).
And lastly: Fresno dad suddenly deported
Luis Arreguin stands at the Cathedral of Mexicali, in Mexicali, Baja California, Mexico, on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Daniel Resendiz for CalMatters
Luis Arreguin, a 54-year-old Fresno resident, was on his way to work as a skilled laborer on Oct. 1 when federal immigration enforcement agents arrested him. Sixteen days later, agents deported him to Mexico — where he hasn’t been since he was a kid — in a stunning example of the dizzying speed in which Trump’s deportation machine operates. Said Arreguin: “My whole life got destroyed.” Read more (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/deportation-after-fresno-sweep/) from CalMatters’ Wendy Fry.

IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

Meet the Berkeley IGS Poll Director
Read Mark DiCamillo's bio here. (https://igs.berkeley.edu/people/mark-dicamillo)
The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).
IGS Poll (2016 - current) and California Field Poll data (1950's to 2015) can be downloaded from UC Berkeley Dataverse (https://datasets.lib.berkeley.edu/dataverse/igs).

Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

Meet the Berkeley IGS Poll Director
Read Mark DiCamillo's bio here. (https://igs.berkeley.edu/people/mark-dicamillo)
The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).
IGS Poll (2016 - current) and California Field Poll data (1950's to 2015) can be downloaded from UC Berkeley Dataverse (https://datasets.lib.berkeley.edu/dataverse/igs).
Contact: igs@berkeley.edu (mailto:igs@berkeley.edu), 510-642-4465; Mark Di Camillo, Berkeley IGS Poll Director,

2026 California Prop 1 guide: Affordable rentals get $7.2 billion of the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop 1’s supporters stress “no new taxes,” which is true. The General Fund would still repay $10 billion at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Here is what that money buys, and why the $1.25 billion veterans’ share costs the state nothing directly.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 17, 2026
