California's Proposition 1 is asking voters to borrow $11.25 billion for affordable rental housing, homebuyers and veterans' home loans.
Proposition 1 would let California borrow $11.25 billion by selling general obligation bonds. Ten billion dollars would go to 11 existing state housing programs and be repaid from the General Fund, mostly to build and preserve apartments rented to low-income households, with the rest for homebuyer help, infrastructure, and farmworker, student and tribal housing. The other $1.25 billion would fund CalVet home loans, which veterans repay through their mortgage payments. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years, roughly a quarter of 1% of the General Fund, and estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental units and help up to 40,000 households with homeownership. The measure creates no new tax; the debt is paid from the state's existing revenue.
The Affordable Housing Bond under Proposition 1 is sending $7.2 billion of its $11.25 billion to rental housing, led by $5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. Prop 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/) placed on the ballot by SB 417, which the Legislature passed and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on June 25. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the third California measure numbered Proposition 1 to borrow for housing since 2018, following the $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond of 2018 and the $6.38 billion behavioral health bond voters approved by 26,223 votes in March 2024. PPIC's September survey found 55% yes and 43% no. No argument against it was filed and no opposition committee exists; the Yes side reports $7.9 million from top donors, including Airbnb, two carpenters' councils, Building a Better California and nonprofit housing developers. This explainer covers where each dollar goes, the veterans' loan bond, the Legislature's power to move money between programs, the cost, the earlier Prop 1s, the money, the argument and the polling.

This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf) has two parts. The first adds Part 16.1 to the Health and Safety Code, creating the Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 and authorizing $10 billion in bonds that are "a valid and binding general obligation of the state," with "the full faith and credit of the state … pledged" to repay them. The second adds an article to the Military and Veterans Code authorizing $1.25 billion in veterans' bonds for the farm and home loan program the Department of Veterans Affairs runs under the Veterans' Farm and Home Purchase Act of 1974. Both sets of bonds are sold over time by state finance committees as programs ask for cash, so the state does not borrow the full amount at once.
Section 54054 divides the $10 billion into 11 lines, each assigned to a program already in state law. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/title-summary.htm) groups them as $5.1 billion for multifamily rental housing, $2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate or preserve affordable housing and provide supportive housing, $1.1 billion for homeownership, $1 billion for farmworker, tribal and student housing, $500 million for infrastructure and $200 million for local programs. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) combines the first two into a single $7.2 billion for affordable multifamily housing. The summary also notes that the money can finance "housing development projects seeking federal tax credits," and the LAO expects most of it to be "used together with other government monies."
Prop 1's $7.2 billion for rental housing runs mostly through the Multifamily Housing Program:
The largest line, $5.1 billion, goes to the Department of Housing and Community Development's Multifamily Housing Program, which lends to developers of new and renovated apartments in exchange for rent limits. The LAO describes these as "low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost," with units generally reserved for low-income households "for a period of 55 years." Prop 1 adds one condition of its own: at least 10% of the assisted units in each development must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
A further $1.15 billion is set aside for supportive housing, where residents get on-site services such as mental health and substance use counseling. The administering agency must offer capitalized operating subsidy reserves for those units, money set aside up front to cover the gap between what very low-income tenants can pay and what the building costs to run. 2026 California Prop 1 guide: Affordable rentals get $7.2 billion of the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop 1’s supporters stress “no new taxes,” which is true. The General Fund would still repay $10 billion at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Here is what that money buys, and why the $1.25 billion veterans’ share costs the state nothing directly.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 17, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California's Proposition 1 is asking voters to borrow $11.25 billion for affordable rental housing, homebuyers and veterans' home loans.
Proposition 1 would let California borrow $11.25 billion by selling general obligation bonds. Ten billion dollars would go to 11 existing state housing programs and be repaid from the General Fund, mostly to build and preserve apartments rented to low-income households, with the rest for homebuyer help, infrastructure, and farmworker, student and tribal housing. The other $1.25 billion would fund CalVet home loans, which veterans repay through their mortgage payments. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years, roughly a quarter of 1% of the General Fund, and estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental units and help up to 40,000 households with homeownership. The measure creates no new tax; the debt is paid from the state's existing revenue.
The Affordable Housing Bond under Proposition 1 is sending $7.2 billion of its $11.25 billion to rental housing, led by $5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. Prop 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/) placed on the ballot by SB 417, which the Legislature passed and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on June 25. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the third California measure numbered Proposition 1 to borrow for housing since 2018, following the $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond of 2018 and the $6.38 billion behavioral health bond voters approved by 26,223 votes in March 2024. PPIC's September survey found 55% yes and 43% no. No argument against it was filed and no opposition committee exists; the Yes side reports $7.9 million from top donors, including Airbnb, two carpenters' councils, Building a Better California and nonprofit housing developers. This explainer covers where each dollar goes, the veterans' loan bond, the Legislature's power to move money between programs, the cost, the earlier Prop 1s, the money, the argument and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf) has two parts. The first adds Part 16.1 to the Health and Safety Code, creating the Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 and authorizing $10 billion in bonds that are "a valid and binding general obligation of the state," with "the full faith and credit of the state … pledged" to repay them. The second adds an article to the Military and Veterans Code authorizing $1.25 billion in veterans' bonds for the farm and home loan program the Department of Veterans Affairs runs under the Veterans' Farm and Home Purchase Act of 1974. Both sets of bonds are sold over time by state finance committees as programs ask for cash, so the state does not borrow the full amount at once.
Section 54054 divides the $10 billion into 11 lines, each assigned to a program already in state law. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/title-summary.htm) groups them as $5.1 billion for multifamily rental housing, $2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate or preserve affordable housing and provide supportive housing, $1.1 billion for homeownership, $1 billion for farmworker, tribal and student housing, $500 million for infrastructure and $200 million for local programs. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) combines the first two into a single $7.2 billion for affordable multifamily housing. The summary also notes that the money can finance "housing development projects seeking federal tax credits," and the LAO expects most of it to be "used together with other government monies."
Prop 1's $7.2 billion for rental housing runs mostly through the Multifamily Housing Program:
The largest line, $5.1 billion, goes to the Department of Housing and Community Development's Multifamily Housing Program, which lends to developers of new and renovated apartments in exchange for rent limits. The LAO describes these as "low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost," with units generally reserved for low-income households "for a period of 55 years." Prop 1 adds one condition of its own: at least 10% of the assisted units in each development must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
A further $1.15 billion is set aside for supportive housing, where residents get on-site services such as mental health and substance use counseling. The administering agency must offer capitalized operating subsidy reserves for those units, money set aside up front to cover the gap between what very low-income tenants can pay and what the building costs to run. New poll shows billionaire tax falling behind as election nears
by
Lynn La (https://calmatters.org/author/lynn-la/)
October 28, 2026 October 27, 2026
A “Tax the Ultra-Rich Now” bus parked in San Francisco on Oct. 3, 2026. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters
Californians’ appetite for a first-in-the-nation wealth tax appears to be waning.
With less than a week before Election Day, support for Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), a proposed billionaire tax, is now under water, according to the latest poll by Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). Published Tuesday, the survey found that 46% of 1,086 likely voters support the tax, while 52% don’t.
That’s a notable change from last month, when Prop. 40 proponents held a slim 52% majority. The billionaire tax is by far the biggest and most expensive fight on the ballot. As of mid-October, wealthy people who oppose it have raised more than $205 million to fight the tax, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who has poured at least $102 million.
Still, Prop. 40 supporters remain undeterred. In response to the PPIC poll, Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union behind the measure, said “large majorities of Democratic voters” continue to support it.
Jimenez , in an email to CalMatters: “Even after months of the most controversial billionaires on the planet spending millions to spread misinformation about it, a clear majority of voters support asking about 250 billionaires to pay a modest, one-time tax to keep … healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.”
Meanwhile, a pair of related ballot measures intended to negate the billionaire tax could go either way.
Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), with 51% in support among those polled, holds onto a narrow lead. It would bar new taxes on personal property and assets and prohibit retroactive taxes. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), which would impose limits to certain new state taxes, appears to be falling short with 48% support.
Voters seem to be more favorable on five other ballot measures (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/last-minute-voter-guide-propositions/). A majority of survey participants said they would vote yes on:
Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/), the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop. 2 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-proposition-2-explained/), which would increase the amount of tax revenue the state can put in savings
Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/), which would permanently extend an income tax for high-earning households
Prop. 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), which would create a $25 billion fund to help homebuyers
Prop. 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), which would dedicate $8 billion in bonds to fund immunology research
As for the governor’s race (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-governor-race-final-stretch/), Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra continues his lead in the polls with PPIC reporting that 61% of likely voters would vote for him, compared to 37% for Republican Steve Hilton.

Other Stories You Should Know
Where Trump’s CA election lawsuit stands
A polling station clerk sanitizes a voting station at the Monsignor Ramon Garcia Recreation Center in East Los Angeles on Nov. 8, 2022. Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters
A federal judge appeared skeptical about the Trump administration’s demands that California set aside 20,000 ballots from alleged noncitizens, but won’t likely rule on the matter until after the Nov. 3 election (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/trump-noncitizen-voting-court/), report CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow and Nigel Duara.
In a potential setback for President Donald Trump, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter on Tuesday raised concerns that the administration’s efforts to stop noncitizens from illegally voting by ordering the state’s elections officials to sequester their ballots could disenfranchise “valid voters.”
Though he’s expected to issue a formal ruling today, Carter’s final ruling might not come until after another hearing that will take place in two weeks. Carter also suggested that his ruling would prohibit federal authorities from threatening elections officials with criminal charges if they didn’t comply with Trump’s demands.
Read more (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/trump-noncitizen-voting-court/).
Could election results help LA fire survivors?
Construction workers build a house in Altadena on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters
Survivors of the Eaton and Palisades fires are running out of money to rebuild their lives, and the outcome of the midterm elections may affect whether federal aid will come (https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/10/la-fire-survivors-federal-disaster-aid/), writes CalMatters’ Levi Sumagaysay.
Nearly two years since the fires ripped through the Los Angeles area, the Trump administration has been slow to release funding to California, and it didn’t include L.A. County wildfire relief in its budget request for Congress this summer.
It’s also unclear when the billions of dollars in long-term disaster recovery money the state has requested will come — if at all. Last week, outlets reported that the Federal Emergency Management Agency told states they will need to handle most disasters themselves (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/20/fema-states-disasters-exclusive-energy-environment-01128120).
U.S. Reps. Judy Chu and Norma Torres, both Southern California Democrats, said that if Democrats flip the House in November, federal aid could roll out to California and other states hit by disaster.
Read more (https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/10/la-fire-survivors-federal-disaster-aid/).
And lastly: Fresno dad suddenly deported
Luis Arreguin stands at the Cathedral of Mexicali, in Mexicali, Baja California, Mexico, on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Daniel Resendiz for CalMatters
Luis Arreguin, a 54-year-old Fresno resident, was on his way to work as a skilled laborer on Oct. 1 when federal immigration enforcement agents arrested him. Sixteen days later, agents deported him to Mexico — where he hasn’t been since he was a kid — in a stunning example of the dizzying speed in which Trump’s deportation machine operates. Said Arreguin: “My whole life got destroyed.” Read more (https://calmatters.org/justice/2026/10/deportation-after-fresno-sweep/) from CalMatters’ Wendy Fry.

Meet the Berkeley IGS Poll Director
Read Mark DiCamillo's bio here. (https://igs.berkeley.edu/people/mark-dicamillo)
The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).
IGS Poll (2016 - current) and California Field Poll data (1950's to 2015) can be downloaded from UC Berkeley Dataverse (https://datasets.lib.berkeley.edu/dataverse/igs).
Contact: igs@berkeley.edu (mailto:igs@berkeley.edu), 510-642-4465; Mark Di Camillo, Berkeley IGS Poll Director,
mdicamillo@berkeley.edu (mailto:mdicamillo@berkeley.edu)

2026 California Prop 1 guide: Affordable rentals get $7.2 billion of the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop 1’s supporters stress “no new taxes,” which is true. The General Fund would still repay $10 billion at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Here is what that money buys, and why the $1.25 billion veterans’ share costs the state nothing directly.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 17, 2026

California's Proposition 1 is asking voters to borrow $11.25 billion for affordable rental housing, homebuyers and veterans' home loans.
Proposition 1 would let California borrow $11.25 billion by selling general obligation bonds. Ten billion dollars would go to 11 existing state housing programs and be repaid from the General Fund, mostly to build and preserve apartments rented to low-income households, with the rest for homebuyer help, infrastructure, and farmworker, student and tribal housing. The other $1.25 billion would fund CalVet home loans, which veterans repay through their mortgage payments. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years, roughly a quarter of 1% of the General Fund, and estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental units and help up to 40,000 households with homeownership. The measure creates no new tax; the debt is paid from the state's existing revenue.
The Affordable Housing Bond under Proposition 1 is sending $7.2 billion of its $11.25 billion to rental housing, led by $5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. Prop 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/) placed on the ballot by SB 417, which the Legislature passed and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on June 25. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the third California measure numbered Proposition 1 to borrow for housing since 2018, following the $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond of 2018 and the $6.38 billion behavioral health bond voters approved by 26,223 votes in March 2024. PPIC's September survey found 55% yes and 43% no. No argument against it was filed and no opposition committee exists; the Yes side reports $7.9 million from top donors, including Airbnb, two carpenters' councils, Building a Better California and nonprofit housing developers. This explainer covers where each dollar goes, the veterans' loan bond, the Legislature's power to move money between programs, the cost, the earlier Prop 1s, the money, the argument and the polling.

The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf) has two parts. The first adds Part 16.1 to the Health and Safety Code, creating the Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 and authorizing $10 billion in bonds that are "a valid and binding general obligation of the state," with "the full faith and credit of the state … pledged" to repay them. The second adds an article to the Military and Veterans Code authorizing $1.25 billion in veterans' bonds for the farm and home loan program the Department of Veterans Affairs runs under the Veterans' Farm and Home Purchase Act of 1974. Both sets of bonds are sold over time by state finance committees as programs ask for cash, so the state does not borrow the full amount at once.
Section 54054 divides the $10 billion into 11 lines, each assigned to a program already in state law. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/title-summary.htm) groups them as $5.1 billion for multifamily rental housing, $2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate or preserve affordable housing and provide supportive housing, $1.1 billion for homeownership, $1 billion for farmworker, tribal and student housing, $500 million for infrastructure and $200 million for local programs. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) combines the first two into a single $7.2 billion for affordable multifamily housing. The summary also notes that the money can finance "housing development projects seeking federal tax credits," and the LAO expects most of it to be "used together with other government monies."
Prop 1's $7.2 billion for rental housing runs mostly through the Multifamily Housing Program:
The largest line, $5.1 billion, goes to the Department of Housing and Community Development's Multifamily Housing Program, which lends to developers of new and renovated apartments in exchange for rent limits. The LAO describes these as "low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost," with units generally reserved for low-income households "for a period of 55 years." Prop 1 adds one condition of its own: at least 10% of the assisted units in each development must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
A further $1.15 billion is set aside for supportive housing, where residents get on-site services such as mental health and substance use counseling. The administering agency must offer capitalized operating subsidy reserves for those units, money set aside up front to cover the gap between what very low-income tenants can pay and what the building costs to run. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. I'm weighing the historical base rate, which shows 88% of bonds passing since 2000, against the risks: the narrow 50.2% pass in March 2024, possible poll overstatement, and opposition from Hilton, some editorial boards, and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Even so, a 60-38 poll points toward likely passage. Next I want to check whether actual results are out yet, so I'm planning to search for Prop 1 result reports and try the NPR, LAist, and other local results pages.
The pre-election evidence is clear. I'll make one more attempt to find actual results from live results pages and news, in case they're already posted.

## Prop. 1: Affordable housing
If voters say yes, Prop.
1 would permit California’s treasurer to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds.
That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes.
The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing.
These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households.
Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless.
The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature.
This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers.
The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election.
Opposition to this bond is minimal.
The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure.

# There’s a $11.25 billion housing bond on the California ballot this November. Here’s what you should know
...
If it passes, Prop.
1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes.
...
California voters approved (by the slimmest of margins) another bond in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans.
That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop.
1.
...
When this measure came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers.

I've got the key pre-election numbers now: PPIC shows Yes at 60% against 38% for No, AIMSA has Yes at 54%, and the Yes campaign has raised over $12 million with no organized opposition. I'm also weighing the Democratic-leaning midterm environment and Becerra's 24-27 point lead.

I'm weighing the historical base rate, which shows 88% of bonds passing since 2000, against the risks: the narrow 50.2% pass in March 2024, possible poll overstatement, and opposition from Hilton, some editorial boards, and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Even so, a 60-38 poll points toward likely passage. Next I want to check whether actual results are out yet, so I'm planning to search for Prop 1 result reports and try the NPR, LAist, and other local results pages.

$500 million for infrastructure related to new housing, such as road and water repairs
$450 million in loans or grants to build or upkeep affordable housing for farmworkers
$350 million to build affordable housing for students, split evenly among the University of California and California State University

- **Official ballot title:** The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 (SB 417, Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026, Limón).
...
- **A vote YES means:** The state may borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds.
This includes about $10 billion in general obligation bonds that would fund affordable housing construction, rehabilitation, and homeownership programs, repaid from the general fund, and about $1.25 billion in revenue bonds funding CalVet home loans, repaid by the veterans who borrow.
- **A vote NO means:** The state does not authorize this borrowing.
...
- **Sponsor/proponent:** Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón (lead Senate author) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (lead Assembly author), with Gov.
...
- **On the ballot because:** The legislature passed SB 417 by the required two-thirds vote and the governor signed it.
Bond acts must go to the voters.
The Senate concurred twenty-nine to two on June 25, 2026.
- **Full legal text:** SB 417, California Legislative Information (leginfo)
- **LAO analysis:** Legislative Analyst’s Office ballot analysis, Proposition 1 (2026)

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> By one measure (https://nlihc.org/gap/state/ca), California is short nearly 1.4 million homes for people earning very low incomes. At the same time, middle-income families also struggle to afford housing in the state, where single-family homes sold for a median price (https://www.car.org/marketdata/data/countysalesactivity) of $887,680 in July.
In response, lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford.
It’s called Proposition 1, or the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income.
Advertisement
Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf), the remaining dollars would be spread across several other initiatives and could subsidize up to 40,000 rental apartments, 2,500 homes for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students:
$1.1 billion to help low- and middle-income families buy homes through direct loans and funds to nonprofits
$500 million for infrastructure related to new housing, such as road and water repairs
$450 million in loans or grants to build or upkeep affordable housing for farmworkers
$350 million to build affordable housing for students, split evenly among the University of California and California State University
$200 million available for tribal members to use to build or repair housing
$200 million available to city and county governments and other entities hoping to pilot programs to build low-cost housing

Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> When lawmakers voted to put this funding on the ballot this year, the votes were split almost entirely among party lines, with state Democrats in support.
Advertisement
“Through this historic bond, we’re giving voters the opportunity to help more Californians achieve homeownership, expand access to affordable housing, and give more families a real shot at the California Dream,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said about the proposition in June.
The bill to put this item on the ballot also was widely supported by organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments, including San Diego, Orange and Santa Barbara counties.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Republicans, who represented all of the votes against Proposition 1, said on the legislative floor that the state instead should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
“We know the cost of building in California is extraordinarily, exponentially higher than it needs to be,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a Republican who represents cities and towns just east of San Diego. “We need reforms first before we take out the credit card and borrow money.”
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The bill to fund these programs initially was introduced in the Legislature last year. Lawmakers noted that the state housing department has estimated that builders will need to construct 2.5 million new homes by 2031 to keep up with demand, and that a little less than half of these homes need to be affordable to low-income families.

Prediction markets put Prop 1 at roughly 84 to 92 percent to pass, averaging about 88. On the opposition side, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, some Republican lawmakers, Hilton, and a few editorial boards are against it, but there's no organized No campaign and no money behind them.

I'm checking the poll coverage next: PPIC shows 60-38 in October and AIMSA 54% yes, but the IGS survey doesn't seem to include Prop 1. I'm also confirming the measure is actually on the ballot, which it is.

I'm going to check how well PPIC's final polls matched results on past California bond measures, using the 2024 Props 2 and 4 and the March 2024 Prop 1, to gauge how much to trust the current 60-38 lead.

I'm checking how accurate PPIC's past polls were on bond measures. The March 2024 Prop 1 came in around 50% yes against a poll that showed more support, so the final lead tends to overstate the result by several points. Even a similar miss would still leave the current 60-38 lead passing.

I'm comparing the historical poll misses: the worst overstatement I can find is about 8 points, on the March 2020 Prop 13, which was a very different primary electorate. Starting from PPIC's 60% yes, a miss that large would still leave the measure passing, so I'd put the chance of a No outcome at only around 3 to 6 percent.

I'm going to check whether the results are already posted, trying Ballotpedia and a few news sites, since the state election results page is blocked.

Prediction markets put Prop 1 at roughly 84–92% to pass, with Howard Jarvis opposing it without funding a campaign. Next I'm checking Ballotpedia and the NPR/AP results page for a posted outcome or more polling.

content.thinking:
Prediction markets put Prop 1 at roughly 84 to 92 percent to pass, averaging about 88. On the opposition side, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, some Republican lawmakers, Hilton, and a few editorial boards are against it, but there's no organized No campaign and no money behind them.

I'm checking the poll coverage next: PPIC shows 60-38 in October and AIMSA 54% yes, but the IGS survey doesn't seem to include Prop 1. I'm also confirming the measure is actually on the ballot, which it is.

I'm going to check how well PPIC's final polls matched results on past California bond measures, using the 2024 Props 2 and 4 and the March 2024 Prop 1, to gauge how much to trust the current 60-38 lead.

I'm checking how accurate PPIC's past polls were on bond measures. The March 2024 Prop 1 came in around 50% yes against a poll that showed more support, so the final lead tends to overstate the result by several points. Even a similar miss would still leave the current 60-38 lead passing.

I'm comparing the historical poll misses: the worst overstatement I can find is about 8 points, on the March 2020 Prop 13, which was a very different primary electorate. Starting from PPIC's 60% yes, a miss that large would still leave the measure passing, so I'd put the chance of a No outcome at only around 3 to 6 percent.

I'm going to check whether the results are already posted, trying Ballotpedia and a few news sites, since the state election results page is blocked.

Prediction markets put Prop 1 at roughly 84–92% to pass, with Howard Jarvis opposing it without funding a campaign. Next I'm checking Ballotpedia and the NPR/AP results page for a posted outcome or more polling.

# School bonds usually are a cinch in California — what happened this time?
Not this election.
As the state slowly tallies the returns from Super Tuesday, the numbers are painting a decidedly unfamiliar picture: Proposition 13, the sweeping $15 billion bond for school construction, was trailing late Thursday with only 44.6% approval.
It threatened to become the first state bond measure rejected by voters in nearly three decades.
Meanwhile, at the district level, some 70% of the 100-plus local K-12 school bond measures appeared bound for failure or too close to call, according to a CalMatters tally of early results.
With roughly 3.5 million votes still to be counted, the tally could take weeks to become conclusive, and updated returns have shown Prop.
13 gaining, slightly.
(Early returns tend to skew conservative in California, and many Democrats voted at the last minute, waiting to see whether their chosen presidential nominees would drop out.)
But at the moment, Prop.
13 needs at least 58% of the outstanding vote for passage.
And the current numbers — which could impact decisions on whether to put bond measures on the November ballot — so far contrast sharply with past elections: In the 2018 midterms, voters approved 80% of the 105 measures on local ballots.
Since 1998, voters have passed five state school bonds, including a $9 billion measure in 2016 that Gov.
Jerry Brown opposed.

I'm noting that this measure drew organized opposition from both the left and the right, and that a lower-turnout March primary with more Republican voters may have skewed things further.

I'm checking the 2020 March Prop 13 result against PPIC's February poll, where Yes was at 51% and fell to 47% on election day. I'm also comparing the November 2024 Prop 2 poll (52-46 Yes) with its actual 58.6%, which the poll understated, and noting that the November 2024 Prop 4 poll (60-38) landed almost exactly on the result.

I'm weighing whether any post-election results exist, since the answer hinges on whether Prop 1 actually passed. I'm going to search again with different phrasing, trying names of later ballot measures and election-night headlines, to see if the results from November 4 are in the index.

PPIC's 60–38 forecast for the 2024 Prop 4 climate bond landed close to the actual 59.8%, while the 2020 and March 2024 primaries missed by more on lower-turnout electorates. I'm running one last search for post-election coverage.

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 1
YES ON PROP. 1: AFFORDABLE HOMES FOR VETERANS, SENIORS, PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES AND WORKING FAMILIES-WITHOUT RAISING TAXES
All Californians deserve a safe and affordable place to call home, but California has a housing shortage that is driving the nation’s worst housing affordability crisis. More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.
Prop. 1 gives Californians the opportunity to:
Fast-track housing production;
Provide housing to working families, veterans, people with disabilities and seniors;
Help prevent homelessness by keeping our most vulnerable neighbors in their homes;
Expands homeownership opportunities;
Maintains strict fiscal accountability and transparency with NO NEW TAXES.
PROP. 1 HONORS OUR VETERANS
Dedicates $1.25 billion solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership opportunities through the existing CalVet Home Loan Program, which has already helped almost a million veterans and their families.
“California has one of the largest populations of homeless veterans in the nation. After their service, our veterans deserve a place to call home. Prop. 1 delivers on that promise.”-Michael Blecker, President, CA Association of Veteran Service Agencies
PROP. 1 BUILDS HOMES LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES CAN AFFORD
Prop. 1 jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes across California, quickly turning stalled construction into move-in ready homes. The teacher in your child’s classroom, the firefighter who protects your neighborhood, first-time homebuyers, low- and middle-income Californians, and the nurse at your local hospital can no longer afford to live in most California communities. Prop. 1 builds more homes working people can actually afford.
NO NEW TAXES-STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY
Prop. 1 doesn’t raise taxes and every dollar comes with strict accountability and public reporting. Voters will be able to see exactly how many homes get built, where, and at what cost. Prop. 1 unlocks federal matching funds, bringing tax dollars we send to Washington back home to California.
PROP. 1 HELPS SENIORS, VETERANS & OUR MOST VULNERABLE
Prop. 1 creates and preserves housing to help those who are one crisis away from homelessness stay off the streets, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, veterans, at risk and foster youth, and people with disabilities who all deserve safe and stable homes.
PROP. 1 INVESTS IN COMMUNITIES & ESSENTIAL WORKERS
Quality, affordable housing is the foundation of thriving communities. Prop. 1 strengthens that foundation by helping essential workers-from firefighters and teachers to nurses-afford to live in the communities they serve. Working families and essential workers across California are being priced out and left behind. Prop. 1 enables the construction of affordable housing for these essential workers who dedicate their lives to our communities.
YES ON PROP. 1: SUPPORTED BY VETERANS, SENIORS, TEACHERS, FIREFIGHTERS, AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES including Habitat for Humanity California, California Alliance for Retired Americans, Housing California, California Housing Consortium, California Alliance of Child and Family Services.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 1, Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond, to honor those veterans who served; provide safe and stable housing to California’s most vulnerable; guarantee strict fiscal accountability with no new taxes; and build the affordable homes all Californians deserve.

There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.

See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41

Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

How this is built
Proposition 1 is forecast as a housing measure whose Yes vote leans Democratic . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further.
